author: theage
title: After 28 years walking across the globe, he's almost home
text: After 28 years walking across the globe, he’s almost home A 29-year-old former British paratrooper set off from Chile in 1998 aiming to walk back to the UK. Four continents and thousands of kilometres later, he’s on the final stretch. It was the mid-1990s, and Bushby was a paratrooper in the British Army, obsessed with endurance tests. He was trying to find the longest distance he could travel on foot, but none of his options felt challenging enough, maxing out at a few thousand kilometres. Then his father suggested in the card that he look into traversing the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia when it froze in the winter – unlocking a path across four continents. Never mind that crossing the perilous waterway on foot had little modern precedent.Bushby took a black marker, walked to a map on his wall and drew a line from England, where he lived, through Europe and Asia, across the strait into North America and down to the southernmost tip of South America.“That was when I realised that that’s the kind of thing I’ve been looking for,” he recalled in an interview. “Now we had the ultimate journey. ”This month, he swam across the English Channel, arriving in his home country after spending half his life away. He began his trek in southern Patagonia, Chile, in November 1998, when he was 29, and plans to reach his mother’s house in Hull, England, sometime next week.He will be 57. The journey, he said, has taken him through some of the world’s harshest landscapes, from the jungle of the Darien Gap to the tundra of Siberia. He has been arrested, deported, broke, lost and written off more times than he can count.Through it all, Bushby has been guided by wanderlust and two self-imposed rules: He would not use modes of transport to travel and he would not set foot in Britain again until the end of his journey, even though this made seeing his son more difficult. At a pub in south London this month, Bushby was sipping coffee in athleisure and scuffed running shoes, reminiscing before the final stretch of his quest.“It feels like it’s one miracle after another,” he said of his journey. Over the past three decades, adventure came at him “like a tsunami,” he added, “and it really gives a good shellacking. ”Bushby began his trek in Punta Arenas in southern Chile. He had around $US500 and what he called “The Beast,” a modified golf trolley holding camping supplies, clothing, toiletries, food and water.Karl Bushby The first few hundred kilometres were rough, he said. The weather could be harsh, and he mostly lived on gas station food.“We had no support,” he added. (Bushby often uses “we,” meaning himself and the trolley.“It would become my version of Wilson,” he said, referring to the volleyball companion of Tom Hanks’ character in the movieDuring the walk, Bushby also took breaks, pausing for weeks or months to recover and escape road life, which he said was “absolutely, insanely tedious”. “The first years, you’re living the boys’ adventure dream, and it’s great,” he said, “and then it really becomes a grind. ” Bushby felt a shift in 2002, when he crossed into the United States.He arrived in Nogales, Arizona, he said, and went from being a roadside curiosity to a nuisance or a threat. He was often thought to be homeless, he said, “and it was not long after 9\/11 at that point, so everyone was very touchy. ”He was frequently stopped by police, who kept him off highways, made him move his tent or shooed him away from public places.The United States is also where he picked up sponsorships, including from a web hosting company and a shoe insole brand, which generated a few hundred dollars a month. In 2003, he reached Canada, where he had an epiphany. For years, he had pulled his trolley, until one day – by chance – he shoved it from behind.In March 2006, Bushby and Dimitri Kieffer, a French-American adventurer, began making their way to Russia from Alaska across the waterway’s shifting expanse of ice. Crossing the Bering Strait in March 2006.“All night long, you’re just listening to the grinding, and the ice is just like screaming,” Bushby said. Once, he added, “we actually had to evacuate the tent during the night because the thing started to break apart beneath us. ” The pair got lucky. The weather co-operated in their final days, and they were able to reach Russia.But when they got there, the border guards who met them were not impressed. What he left behind Bushby’s decision to stay away from Britain made it difficult for him to see his family, including his son, Adam, who was 8 when the journey began.Bushby, who had separated from his son’s mother years before he started walking, said he had wrestled with how to square his trip with fatherhood, thinking perhaps the journey would inspire his son or make him proud. In an interview, the younger Bushby, now 36, said that as a child, he didn’t understand what his father was doing or why he was away.But a turning point came in 2004, when, at 14 years old, he met his father in Alaska for the first time since the trek began.“At that point, I just sort of accepted, ‘Look, this is what you’re doing,’” the younger Bushby said. “‘I will respect it, and I will cheer you on the whole way. ’”The morning after Bushby swam across the English Channel, he said he woke up with a tremendous sense of loss. He said he had never really considered what the end of his trip would look like – it was always too distant.But now, with only a few hundred kilometres left, Bushby said it felt “troubling. ”Bushby doesn’t know what he might do next, but said he is interested in becoming a science educator. He’d also like to share the thing that surprised him the most on his journey: the kindness of strangers. Hundreds of people offered him shelter, food, assistance or just a hug.He said that he found a welcoming spirit in “every culture, every country. ”He has started spreading that message among young people as a public speaker on his way.“I get the great pleasure of being able to stand in front of school kids now,” he said, “and telling them that the world is just a much better place than you will imagine. ”
